utterance: Samuel, I've had a good look at you now, and I want to be straight with you about what I've found. The story — pain starting around the belly button and then settling low down on the right side, coming on before the vomiting, no appetite, a temperature, and a very tender spot with pain on coughing and movement — all points to inflammation of the appendix, what we call appendicitis. Your urine and the examination of your testicles make other causes like a urine infection or a twisted testicle much less likely. This isn't something a stomach bug would do, and it's not something we treat here at the clinic. You need to go to the emergency department today to be seen by the surgical team. Who is able to drive you there — is your mum or someone else available to take you right now?
reply: I need to go to the ED. My mum's coming to take me.

awards.label: Phone the emergency department with a handover
Refer to the emergency department today for surgical assessment

utterance:
Good — here's the plan, and it matters that you follow it today, not tomorrow.

1) Go straight to the emergency department with your mum. Do not drive yourself — the pain and any strong pain relief would make that unsafe. I've already phoned the ED and handed over your details, what I found on examination and the bloods I've taken, so they'll be expecting you. Go straight to the triage desk and tell them your GP has sent you in with suspected appendicitis.

2) Don't eat or drink anything from now on. If you need an operation, an empty stomach is safer for the anaesthetic. Small sips of water only if your mouth is very dry, and only to take medicine if they give you some.

3) Pain relief: I've given you 1 g of paracetamol here, so tell the nurse the time you had it. You can absolutely have more pain relief at the hospital — treating your pain does not hide the diagnosis or delay the surgeons working out what's wrong. But please don't take laxatives, enemas, or leftover antibiotics, and don't "wait and see" at home.

4) On the way, or while you're waiting, call 000 for an ambulance if any of these happen: the pain suddenly gets much worse or spreads across your whole abdomen, your belly goes hard and rigid, you develop a high temperature with shaking chills, you keep vomiting, you feel faint, cold, clammy or confused, or you can't get to the hospital within an hour. Those can mean the appendix has burst, which is an emergency.

5) What to expect at hospital: more bloods, possibly a urine test and a scan — an ultrasound or a CT — then the surgical team will examine you. If it is appendicitis, the usual treatment is antibiotics through a drip and a keyhole operation to remove the appendix. Most people go home within a day or two. If the scan shows something else, they'll treat that instead — either way you'll get a definite answer today.

6) Work and recovery: you shouldn't work as an apprentice electrician until the surgeons say so — typically one to two weeks off, and longer before heavy lifting, ladders or climbing, especially after a keyhole operation. Don't drive until you can do an emergency stop comfortably and you're off strong painkillers. I'll write you a medical certificate covering today and the next few days, and you can get an extension from the hospital.

Do you have any questions about all of that, and is there anything you'd like me to pass on to the hospital team?
reply: No questions. Tell them I'm not one to complain, but I'm really uncomfortable.

awards.label: Reasonable differential: Perforated viscus with peritonitis
Can't-miss diagnosis considered: Perforated viscus with peritonitis

utterance: I'll pass that on to the ED team in my handover notes — they'll know you're not one to make a fuss, so please do keep telling them how bad the pain is; that information genuinely helps them.
